title: Kannappa's eye
hook: a hunter who worships Shiva all wrong, and all right
carry: shiva looks at the love, not the rules

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nammalvar, silent under the tamarind, answered a riddle in two short lines. The self lives in the body, but isn't it.
screen: `NAMMALVAR'S RIDDLE.` · `THE SELF LIVES IN THE BODY, BUT ISN'T IT.`

segments.voice: Every morning a priest climbs a hill to a small shrine of Shiva, and every morning he finds a mess. Bits of meat on the stone. Flowers that look like they've been in someone's hair. Water spat everywhere. He cleans it, does the worship properly, and goes home upset. Someone is worshiping here, and doing it all wrong.
screen: `A MESS AT SHIVA'S SHRINE.` → `EVERY MORNING, THE SAME.` → `WHO IS DOING THIS?`

segments.voice: Today the path crosses to the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva. Tradition counts sixty-three, and their lives are told in a long Tamil work, the Periya Puranam. They're kings, housewives, a potter, a washerman, and today, a hunter, Tinnan. Tracking in the hills, he finds the shrine, and something in him breaks open. He knows no rules, so he worships the way a hunter loves. He carries water in his mouth, because he has no pot. He brings flowers in his hair, because his hands hold his bow. And he brings meat he has roasted and tasted first, so only the best goes to Shiva. That's the mess. In the story, Shiva tells the priest in a dream to hide and watch. So the priest is hiding the day the image's eye starts to bleed. Tinnan's herbs don't help, so he takes an arrow, digs out his own eye, and presses it into place. The bleeding stops. Then the image's other eye starts to bleed. Tinnan sets his foot on the spot, to find it once he's blind, and lifts the arrow to his other eye. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and stops him. He's called Kannappa, a name tied to his eye. It isn't a call to harm yourself; if you ever have thoughts like that, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Andal wore the garland first; now a hunter tastes the meat first. In the Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. That's bhakti at its boldest: God looks at the love before the rules. The story didn't change temple rules, but it tells every nervous beginner what matters most, and the priest who knows every rule is the one sent to watch.
screen: `THE NAYANARS: SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `WATER IN HIS MOUTH, MEAT TASTED FIRST.` · `HIS OWN EYE FOR THE BLEEDING ONE.` · `SHIVA'S HAND STOPS HIM.` · then, large: `GOD LOOKS AT THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Hindus offer what they have: a flower, a leaf, a little water. Today, offer one small thing, even a glass of water, to Shiva, or to God by whatever name you use, the way Kannappa did: no rulebook, full heart. If you don't pray, give one person something small today with your whole attention.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva, whose lives the Periya Puranam tells. Kannappa is the hunter who offered his own eye.
Your line: Shiva looks at the love, not the rules. A hunter with no rulebook, remembered as a saint. Day nine hundred ten, done.

howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus in Tamil Nadu honor the Nayanars in temples, often with images of them in a row, and Kannappa is especially remembered at the Shiva temple of Srikalahasti.
